source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-002) was run on the canonical Daw two-step task as a text prompt. Its stay pattern looked model-based: after a rare transition with reward it switched away.
numbers: 200 simulations, 20 trials each. Stay prob fell after rare+rewarded (t(1982)=-6.16, p<.001) and rose after rare+unrewarded (t(1814)=2.33, p=.01). No fitted model-based weight reported.
limits: Sign-pattern test only, no mixture fit. The same paper shows GPT-3 fails the Cognitive Reflection Test, and small prompt changes break vignette tasks. History is in the prompt, so the model may copy the transition story, not plan.
agent_relevance: A model-based looking choice is cheap when the full history of (action, state, reward) lines sits in context. Keep that history explicit and ordered in the agent memory.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) GPT-3 two-step prompt design
finding: The prompt gave a cover story, the last three trips as text lines (boarded X, arrived at X, traded with D, got treasures), then asked for the next choice. Transitions stayed 0.7/0.3 and alien reward probabilities drifted in 0.25-0.75.
numbers: 3 prior trials per prompt; 20 repetitions of both stages per simulation; 200 simulations.
limits: Only 3 trials of history per prompt, so the model sees almost no learning curve. Far from the 200-trial human task.
agent_relevance: Shows a minimal memory format that exposes transition structure: one line per trip with chosen state vs reached state.

source: Coda-Forno, Binz, Wang, Schulz (2024) CogBench: a large language model walks into a psychology lab
finding: CogBench scores 35 LLMs on ten behavioral metrics. One metric, model-basedness, comes from the two-step task: a regression of stay on reward x common/rare transition. Bigger models are more model-based.
numbers: 35 LLMs. Parameter count effect on model-basedness beta=0.481 +/-0.22, z=4.2, p<0.001. Training-set size and code training had no significant effect. Proprietary models that solve the task are at least on par with humans; GPT-4 is above human level.
limits: Model-basedness is a regression weight on the transition x reward term, not proof of planning. Most models are not human-like on most behavioral metrics.
agent_relevance: Model-based style choice scales with model size, so a small driver model may need the structure written out for it.

source: Coda-Forno et al. (2024) CogBench prompt effects on model-basedness
finding: Two prompts raised model-basedness. Chain-of-thought raised it by 64.59 percent and take-a-step-back by 118.59 percent relative to base models. CoT helped probabilistic reasoning more (+9.01 percent) than step-back (+3.10 percent).
numbers: Relative increases averaged over the models tested with each prompt. CoT +64.59 pct; step-back +118.59 pct model-basedness.
limits: Relative increases from a low base; absolute values per model are in the paper's Figure 6. Not a planning test.
agent_relevance: Abstracting the problem to its structure (step-back) is the best prompt lever for model-based behavior found here. Add a structure-summary step before action choice.

source: Coda-Forno et al. (2024) CogBench RLHF and code tuning
finding: RLHF models are more human-like and better calibrated. Open-source models are less risk-prone. Code fine-tuning did not help model-basedness or performance.
numbers: Multilevel regression over 35 LLMs, nested by base model.
limits: Many proprietary models are opaque, so size and data effects are partly guesses.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a code-tuned driver to do better at structure-learning tasks.

source: Momennejad, Hasanbeig, Vieira Frujeri, Sharma, Ness, Jojic, Palangi, Larson (2023) Evaluating cognitive maps and planning in LLMs with CogEval
finding: Eight-plus LLMs were tested on cognitive maps and planning built from human revaluation tasks (shortcut, detour, reward revaluation, transition revaluation, policy revaluation) across 6 graphs and 3 domains. Competence only on simple tasks where routes could be memorized. Failures: hallucinated edges, overly long paths, loops.
numbers: 30 runs per prompt, temperatures 0, 0.5, 1. GPT-4 mean scores: 1stepPath 0.99, 2stepPath 0.82, 3stepPath 0.55, nstepPath 0.47, rewardReval 0.67, transReval 0.60, nonteleDetour 0.55, nonteleShortcut 0.56. Smaller models mostly 0.1-0.4.
limits: Scores are mean accuracy 0-1. Temperature and LLM-by-temperature effects not significant (chi2(11)=1.28, p=.53). 2023 models; no reasoning models tested.
agent_relevance: The failure profile is what a missing transition model gives. The agent should store the edge list explicitly and validate each step against it.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) CogEval policy revaluation
finding: Policy revaluation, the case that separates SR-style caching from full model-based planning, was the hardest condition. Most models scored near zero.
numbers: GPT-4 0.21, GPT-3.5 0.18, davinci-003 0.13, Claude-1 0.28; Pythia-20B and Cohere 0.00.
limits: Task wording is text; a low score may partly reflect parsing and prompt style.
agent_relevance: Re-deriving a plan after the goal or policy changes is where bare models break. The scaffold should force a recompute, not reuse a cached route.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) CogEval BFS/DFS instruction and failure rate
finding: Adding breadth-first or depth-first search instructions helped only slightly. Finding a shortest path one cluster away, GPT-4 succeeded in 0 of 30 runs at temperature 0 and at most 10 percent at other temperatures.
numbers: 30 runs per prompt and temperature. BFS helped within-cluster at temp 0; only BFS at temp 0.5 helped 1-cluster-away.
limits: Single community graph for the instruction test; GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Telling the model the algorithm in words is weak. Better run the search outside the model on a stored graph.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) CogEval worked-example CoT on shortcuts
finding: Worked-example CoT gave perfect scores on one shortcut variant for the two strongest models but not for others, and not on the teleporting version, which looks like memorized procedure, not map understanding.
numbers: nonteleShortcutCoT: GPT-4 1.00, GPT-3.5 1.00, davinci-003 0.09, Claude-1 0.58. teleShortcutCoT: GPT-4 0.50, GPT-3.5 0.50.
limits: Single prompt family; tele and non-tele versions differ in structure.
agent_relevance: A worked example fixes a task family. It is not a general map.

source: Mondal, Webb, Momennejad (2025) Improving planning with LLMs: a modular agentic architecture (MAP), Nature Communications
finding: MAP splits planning into LLM modules: action proposer, monitor that rejects invalid moves, state predictor (world model), state evaluator, task decomposer and orchestrator. This is model-based tree search with the LLM as transition model. It removed invalid-action hallucination.
numbers: Graph traversal: Valuepath 100 percent solved; zero invalid actions on all four graph tasks. Tower of Hanoi 3-disk: nearly seven-fold gain over GPT-4 zero-shot; best of 5 runs 100 percent; 4-disk OOD baselines near 0 percent while MAP made no invalid moves. PlanBench Logistics: MAP 24 vs CoT 17, ICL 12, zero-shot 7; Mystery Blocksworld 27.4 vs CoT 10.6. StrategyQA 87.7 +/-0.7 vs CoT 84.7, ToT 81.7, human 87.0.
limits: Many LLM calls per problem (cost). Best-of-5 numbers are optimistic. Transfer: n7tree 80 vs CoT 65, n15star 12.2 vs 1.4. Uses no SR or cached values.
agent_relevance: Closest working design to our need: separate the monitor (validity check against known edges) from the proposer. The monitor alone cut invalid moves to 0.

source: Mondal et al. (2025) MAP ablation
finding: Removing the Monitor raised invalid moves from 0 percent to 31 percent and cut solved problems. Tree search alone (ToT) did not explain MAP's results.
numbers: Ablation without Monitor: 31 percent invalid moves vs 0 percent for other ablations. ToT below MAP on Tower of Hanoi and on the Logistics subset.
limits: Ablation on Tower of Hanoi with GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Keep a validity check as its own step. It is the cheapest piece with the clearest measured gain.

source: Demircan, Saanum, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) Sparse autoencoders reveal temporal difference learning in LLMs
finding: Llama 3 70B solves small in-context RL tasks (two-step task variants, grid world). Sparse autoencoder features track TD error and Q-values. Switching off the TD feature hurt behavior, so it is causal.
numbers: Best SAE feature in block 34 correlates with the Q-learning TD error at r=0.58. SAEs trained with lambda=1e-5, 30 epochs, 18000 residual vectors. A repetition model fit worse than chance (NLL 5745).
limits: One model, small tasks. Correlation to a fitted agent does not rule out other algorithms.
agent_relevance: An LLM can carry a value-update signal inside its activations, not only copy text. The signal is weak, so write values down in memory.

source: Demircan et al. (2024) LLM learns graph structure like a successor representation
finding: Llama 3 70B saw a random walk over a 3-community graph (15 nodes) and predicted the next node. Its hidden features match the successor representation better than a plain transition matrix, and SR TD errors matched much better than a transition-surprise signal.
numbers: 401 observations, 20 runs. Next-state accuracy 24.3 percent vs ceiling 25 percent after about 100 transitions. SAE max r with SR 0.62 vs transition matrix 0.49. TD error max r=0.60 vs transition surprise r=0.18. Lesioning the TD latent in block 64 cut accuracy from 24.3 to 18.9 percent. Bottleneck states linearly decodable from about block 20.
limits: Max correlations over many SAE latents, so selection inflates r. One model, one graph, dense random-walk text.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence that SR-like structure forms in context. Supports storing multi-step 'where this leads' occupancy, not only one-step links.

source: Wang, Blaser, Daneshmand, Zhang (2025) Transformers can learn temporal difference methods for in-context RL
finding: A transformer trained on policy evaluation learns TD learning in its forward pass. Proved by construction for a linear-attention transformer.
numbers: Proof for single-layer linear attention; empirical check with nonlinear TD on randomly generated tasks.
limits: Small synthetic setup, not an LLM. Policy evaluation only, no control.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism for why in-context value learning can work, and a limit: it is shallow and needs clean trajectories.

source: Fang and Rajan (2025) From memories to maps: mechanisms of in-context RL in transformers
finding: A transformer meta-trained on gridworld and tree-maze planning learns in context. It reaches near-max return after one reward exposure and finds shortcuts in over 60 percent of test runs. Its strategy is neither standard model-free nor model-based; it caches intermediate computations in memory tokens.
numbers: Shortcuts in over 60 percent of test simulations; near-maximal return after one reward; tabular Q-learning and DQN on the same data much worse. Representations resemble predictive maps though no such loss was used.
limits: Small meta-trained transformer, not a pretrained LLM. Rodent-style tasks.
agent_relevance: Memory acts as a cache of computed results. Store derived results (routes, values) beside raw events, with the date computed.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with language model is planning with world model (RAP)
finding: The LLM acts as world model (predicts next state) and as agent, with Monte Carlo tree search. This is model-based planning in an LLM loop. On Blocksworld it beats chain-of-thought.
limits: 10-20 search iterations per problem (cost). Reward at later steps sees only the current state, which eases late steps. Toy domain.
agent_relevance: Imagination loops (predict next state, score, back up) cost compute but give real gains on longer plans.

source: Gu, Zhang, Sun, Su (2025) Is your LLM secretly a world model of the internet? WebDreamer
finding: Model-based planning for web agents: an LLM simulates the outcome of each candidate action, scores it, then commits one action. It beats reactive agents and is 4-5 times cheaper than real tree search with backtracking.
numbers: Success rates, reactive / tree search / WebDreamer (GPT-4o): VisualWebArena 17.6 / 26.2 / 23.6; Online-Mind2Web 26.0 / - / 37.0; Mind2Web-Live 20.2 / - / 25.0. Relative gains 34.1, 42.3, 23.8 percent. Tree search used about 3x more steps and 10x latency (Reddit 972 s vs 234 s).
limits: Authors re-implemented all baselines. The 7B Dreamer model gained 4.7, 4.0, 4.8 points over base Qwen2-VL-7B but trails GPT-4o on VWA (21.9 vs 23.6).
agent_relevance: Imagine-before-act is a cheap middle way between pure reaction and live search. Fits the SR idea: predict outcomes without taking the action.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) GAMER: graph-based action-centric memory with episodic reasoning
finding: An LLM agent keeps a graph of past actions. Model-free TD learning gives each action node two values, a suggestion value from successes and an avoidance value from failures, and the agent searches the graph at decision time. A model-free value cache inside an LLM loop.
numbers: Averaged over 4 LLMs and 4 benchmarks: success 31.60 vs vanilla 26.31 (reported +20.81 percent success, +6.17 percent progress relative). Memory baselines: A-Mem 29.07, Reflexion 20.81, Voyager 22.76, MemoryBank 22.30, ReasoningBank 12.58. About 50 percent fewer tokens than A-Mem.
limits: Preprint from the method's authors. Several published memory methods score below vanilla in the same table. Values are one-step TD, not an SR.
agent_relevance: Template for storing what an action led to, with a negative value stream so the agent avoids known dead ends.

source: Parks and Alharthi (2026) Predictive maps of multi-agent reasoning: an SR spectrum for LLM communication topologies
finding: Applies M=(I-gamma P)^-1 to the communication graph of a multi-agent LLM system and reads spectral radius, gap and condition number as failure predictors. Condition number rank-ordered perturbation robustness; spectral radius was inverted for cumulative error.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 12-step state tracking, 100 trials per cell. Spearman rs: condition number +1.0, spectral gap +0.5, spectral radius -1.0. Error amplification chain 2094 vs mesh 1241 vs star 1184. Kruskal-Wallis H=58.02, 188.68, 29.03 (all p<0.001).
limits: Only 3 topologies, so rs of +/-1 rests on 3 points. One 7B model, one task. Authors call it a case study. Linear spectrum missed non-contracting bias drift.
agent_relevance: Possible pre-run check for multi-step agent graphs. Weak evidence; do not rely on it.

source: Immertreu, Schilling, Kinfe, Krauss (2026) Word-class and construction-like structure emerges in neural successor representations trained on natural language
finding: A residual network trained on WikiText-103 to predict successor distributions over words at three horizons recovers parts of speech without labels. Longer horizons agree less with part-of-speech classes.
numbers: At gamma=0.2, K=3: ARI 0.67, NMI 0.60 (noun/verb/adjective); ARI falls below 0.06 at larger K on that subset. Two consensus clusterings agree at ARI 0.93. With 13 POS classes ARI peaks near 0.41 at K near 13. Of 30 clusters, 12 reach purity 1.0.
limits: Small network, one corpus, spaCy as reference. Not an LLM agent study.
agent_relevance: Short horizon SR captures local class; long horizon captures theme. The horizon sets what 'where does this lead' stores.

source: Baumgartner, Spens, Burgess, Manescu (2025) Cognitive maps in language models: a mechanistic analysis of spatial planning
finding: GPT-2 models trained in three regimes learned different algorithms. Random-walk (foraging) training gave a map-like coordinate system; shortest-path training gave a path-dependent shortcut tied to direction tokens.
numbers: Foraging model: 100 percent single-step accuracy at 2-3 steps, 71 percent near 11 steps, over 96 percent past 30 steps. Shortest-path model: 100 percent in distribution, 0 percent for other context lengths. Hybrid kept over 97 percent. Patching: 97.4 percent of trials transferred direction.
limits: Small GPT-2 trained from scratch on grids. Not a pretrained LLM.
agent_relevance: Reward-free exploration data builds a reusable map; goal-only data builds a brittle route habit. Log reward-free observations too.

source: Lampinen, Engelcke, Li, Chaudhry, McClelland (2025) Latent learning: episodic memory complements parametric learning by enabling flexible reuse of experiences
finding: Language models fail to reuse what they saw for a new goal (reversal curse, latent gridworld targets), as in Tolman latent learning. Retrieving past episodes into context fixes much of it, but only if training also had within-episode in-context-learning examples.
numbers: Without in-context-learning sequences in training, even with oracle retrieval: reversals about 12 percent, codebooks about 6 percent, gridworld latent objects fail. With them, retrieval gives large gains on latent test sets.
limits: Retrieval is an oracle, not a learned retriever. Models trained by the authors, not frontier LLMs.
agent_relevance: Latent learning is where SR or model-based storage beats cached values. Keep raw episodes retrievable by possible future use, not only the task they solved.

source: Binz, Akata et al. (2025) Centaur: a foundation model of human cognition
finding: Llama 3.1 70B fine-tuned on Psych-101 (160 experiments, over 60,000 participants, over 10 million choices). In open-loop simulation on the two-step task it produced purely model-free, purely model-based and mixed trajectories like people, and tracked a changed cover story (magic carpets) never in training.
numbers: Two-step task held-out NLL per trial: 0.4998 vs 0.6075 and 0.6043 in the other two columns (lower is better). Economic-game control: humans predicted at 64 percent vs artificial agent 35 percent. Neural alignment: Centaur beat Llama and the cognitive model in accumbens and medial PFC.
limits: Column labels in the supplementary table were not clear in the extracted text; check the Nature version. Fine-tuned on human data, so it predicts human behavior; it is not evidence that the base LLM plans.
agent_relevance: LLMs can model the human model-free/model-based mix when fine-tuned. Not a route for a scaffold-only agent.

source: LAPITHS (2026) Taming the Centaur(s): a framework for a theoretically grounded interpretation of AI cognition claims
finding: A critique run on the two-step task. Retrieval-augmented LLM agents given a reward structure matched Centaur's choice likelihood without fine-tuning, so good fit does not show a cognitive mechanism. It also questions the fMRI alignment claim.
numbers: 150 trials (300 decisions) per model; sampling-based NLL per decision.
limits: Sampling-based NLL, not token likelihood, so the authors call the comparison descriptive. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Behavioral fit on the two-step task is easy with context and retrieval; it cannot show which algorithm runs.

source: Russek, Momennejad, Botvinick, Gershman, Daw (2017) Predictive representations can link model-based RL to model-free mechanisms
finding: Older computational system: SR combined with TD (SR-TD) solves latent learning and reward revaluation without decision-time search, but cannot solve transition revaluation (Tolman detour). SR-MB (recompute M from a learned one-step model at decision time) solves the detour; SR-Dyna replays offline.
numbers: Simulated gridworld agents; SR-TD fails detour, SR-MB succeeds.
limits: Simulations only, tabular states. SR-MB needs matrix recomputation at choice time.
agent_relevance: Cached 'leads to' structure is good for a new goal, bad after the map changes. Mark such caches stale when a transition changes.

source: Kulkarni, Saeedi, Gautam, Gershman (2016) Deep successor reinforcement learning
finding: Deep successor representation learned from pixels in a grid maze and a VizDoom 4-room map. It adapts faster when a distal reward changes because reward and dynamics are factored, and extracts bottleneck subgoals from the SR under a random policy.
numbers: Competitive with DQN on reward over 100k steps (maze) and 180k steps (Doom).
limits: Small environments; gain shown in reward-change tests, not raw learning speed.
agent_relevance: Factor 'what leads where' from 'what is valued'. A changed goal then needs only a new reward vector.

source: Barreto et al. (2017) Successor features for transfer in reinforcement learning
finding: Successor features plus generalized policy improvement let an agent reuse old policies on a new reward with guarantees before learning. On navigation tasks and a simulated robot arm, SFDQN beat DQN trained per task.
numbers: Reacher domain normalized return, where 1 = DQN trained separately per task and 0 = random agent.
limits: Needs rewards linear in known features.
agent_relevance: Class-level 'where this leads' storage transfers when reward changes but dynamics stay fixed.

source: Machado, Bellemare, Bowling (2017) A Laplacian framework for option discovery
finding: Eigenvectors of the successor representation give eigenpurposes, intrinsic rewards from which options are learned without task reward. Tested in tabular domains and Atari 2600. Options that speed planning can hurt exploration; these help both.
numbers: Tabular domains and Atari 2600; no single headline number taken here.
limits: Option learning cost; evidence mainly in small domains.
agent_relevance: SR structure can yield reusable subgoals without reward, a candidate for splitting a big task into stages.

source: Search check 2026-10-31: LLM agent memory built on successor representations
finding: A search for LLM-agent memory using successor representations or predictive maps found none. Only linked work: Parks 2026 (graph diagnostic) and Demircan 2024 (SR-like features inside Llama). The SR review (2402.06590) lists SR uses in decision making and memory but not agent memory.
numbers: About 12 arXiv and web queries; zero direct hits.
limits: Absence of evidence; search covers indexed pages only.
agent_relevance: The SR memory idea is open ground for us. Risk: no measured benefit for LLM agents yet.
